metadata.title: How is students’ motivation related to their performance and anxiety? PISA in Focus #92

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA in Focus uses PISA 2015 questionnaire and assessment data from 55 education systems, which are collected using PISA’s complex, multi-stage sampling design (students nested in schools and education systems). The excerpt does not report whether analysts applied student/sampling weights or replicate weights, nor does it name any weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT). For any re-analysis with PISA microdata, analysts should use the official PISA sampling weights and replicate weights provided in the OECD/IEA data products to obtain correct standard errors under the complex design. Plausible values are typically used for cognitive achievement outcomes in PISA; however, this PISA in Focus primarily reports associations and differences rather than providing a full technical specification in the excerpt.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus #92 summarizes relationships between students’ motivation to achieve and two outcomes: performance in the PISA 2015 assessment and students’ test-related anxiety. Students in 55 education systems responded to five motivation statements (e.g., wanting top grades, wanting to be among the best, seeing oneself as ambitious). Across education systems, the brief reports that motivation is not strongly related to performance at the country level, but within almost every system motivation is positively associated with higher performance; this association is not statistically significant in Belgium and Singapore. The brief also reports that motivation is associated with higher anxiety, with the relationship varying by the type of motivation (extrinsic vs intrinsic) and by country. It further highlights that both motivation and performance are patterned by students’ socio-economic environments, suggesting that contextual factors may partly explain observed associations.
